section_summary: This section begins with the conclusion of a translated interview report on wartime living and working conditions in Japan, covering rationing, air-raid precautions, industrial labor, agriculture, and the decline of small business. It then contains Chinese Communist newspaper analyses of Japanese morale, politics, the Philippines campaign, and Japan’s wartime economy, followed by American diplomatic correspondence and an interview with former Romanian diplomat Victor Gutzulesco about Japan and Manchuria in early 1945. The section ends with a Chungking Embassy despatch forwarding further translations and the opening pages of an article on the Koiso Cabinet’s advisory and planning machinery.

subfiles.title: Continuation of translated interviews on wartime living and economic conditions in Japan
subfiles.about: Interviewees describe housing, fuel, air defenses, industrial labor, farming, and small-business conditions in wartime Japan.
subfiles.summary: The continuation records shortages of clothing, electricity, charcoal, housing, and food, together with rudimentary shelters and frequent air-raid drills. Workers describe long hours, compulsory savings, forced overtime, beatings, labor conscription, dangerous mine work, and declining morale, including a violent Korean labor disturbance. Farmers report fertilizer and labor shortages, compulsory crop deliveries, falling silk production, and growing pessimism about the war, while small merchants describe state-directed mergers and transfers into munitions work.

subfiles.title: Editorial on corruption, black markets, and labor sabotage in Japan
subfiles.doc_type: translated newspaper article; enclosure to despatch no. 264
subfiles.from: Supplement to Giefang Ribao (The Emancipation Daily), translated by the Co-ordinated Translation Center
subfiles.about: A Chinese Communist editorial uses Japanese press admissions to argue that civilian luxury, black markets, absenteeism, and resistance to labor mobilization were weakening Japan's war effort.
subfiles.summary: The article contrasts official praise for mass suicide and patriotic sacrifice with reports of luxury consumption, clandestine textile production, and expensive black-market food. It describes absenteeism, diversion of factory rations, sabotage by adult and child workers, and widespread evasion of women's volunteer service and labor conscription. The writer presents these practices as evidence that much of the Japanese population was resisting the militarized wartime system.

subfiles.title: The Japanese “emancipation” of the Philippines
subfiles.doc_type: translated newspaper article; enclosure to despatch no. 264
subfiles.from: Supplement to Giefang Ribao (The Emancipation Daily), translated by the Co-ordinated Translation Center
subfiles.about: The article attacks Japanese cultural propaganda and economic exploitation in the occupied Philippines.
subfiles.summary: Japanese occupation authorities are described as imposing Japanese language, street names, slogans, songs, and propaganda films while claiming to have emancipated the Filipinos. The article alleges severe exploitation of minerals, falling sugar and coconut production, unemployment, rice shortages, textile scarcity, and rapid inflation. It concludes that worsening conditions and transparently false victory reports had destroyed Filipino confidence in Japanese-sponsored independence.

subfiles.title: Editorial on Japanese naval defeat, war-weariness, and the Cabinet advisory system
subfiles.doc_type: translated editorial; enclosure to despatch no. 264
subfiles.from: Supplement to Giefang Ribao (The Emancipation Daily), translated by the Co-ordinated Translation Center
subfiles.about: The editorial assesses Japan's strategic reverses in the western Pacific and the Koiso government's effort to broaden responsibility through Cabinet advisers.
subfiles.summary: The writer argues that Japanese naval losses near Formosa and the Philippines had shifted naval supremacy to Admiral Nimitz and threatened Japan's southern communications. Growing public pessimism and pressure for compromise are contrasted with Koiso's warnings that defeat would destroy the Japanese nation. The enlarged Cabinet advisory system is portrayed as a heterogeneous coalition of military, financial, bureaucratic, and technical interests likely to deepen rather than solve the government's crisis.

subfiles.title: Philippine independence and anti-Japanese resistance
subfiles.doc_type: translated newspaper article; enclosure to despatch no. 264
subfiles.from: Yu Lu, supplement to Giefang Ribao, translated by the Co-ordinated Translation Center
subfiles.about: Yu Lu links the return of American forces to Filipino guerrilla resistance and the postwar establishment of an independent Philippine republic.
subfiles.summary: The article praises Filipino guerrillas for cooperating with American forces and aiding the Leyte landings, citing Roosevelt and MacArthur in support of their contribution. It reviews prewar independence legislation but criticizes economic provisions that would have protected narrow American agricultural interests. The author argues that genuine independence should conform to international democratic principles and that postwar political authority should belong to those who contributed most to liberation.

subfiles.title: The Philippines in Japan's wartime economic system
subfiles.doc_type: translated newspaper analysis; enclosure to despatch no. 264
subfiles.from: Chinese Communist press article translated by the Co-ordinated Translation Center
subfiles.about: The article evaluates the economic and strategic consequences for Japan of losing the Philippines.
subfiles.summary: The Philippines are depicted as a planned center of colonial light industry and a supplier of copper, iron, chromium, manganese, and other materials to Japanese war industries. Allied reconquest would sever an important maritime route, destroy Japanese investments, and intensify conflict among financial cliques represented in the Koiso Cabinet. Although Japan was attempting to construct a self-sufficient Japan-Manchuria-China bloc and stockpile southern resources, the article contends that petroleum, rubber, metals, and iron ore still made it dependent on the South and explains Japanese offensives toward Guilin and Liuzhou as an effort to preserve an overland supply route.

subfiles.title: The American Landing on Luzon and the Koiso Cabinet
subfiles.doc_type: translated newspaper article; enclosure to despatch no. 264
subfiles.from: Yu Lu, New Intelligence no. 64, supplement to Giefang Ribao
subfiles.about: Yu Lu analyzes the Luzon landing as a military threat to Japan and a political crisis for the Koiso Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: The article predicts fierce Japanese resistance on Luzon but argues that special-attack tactics cannot overcome American superiority in ships, aircraft, armor, and artillery. It describes overlapping Japanese policy bodies, conflict between the Army and financial interests over munitions production, and the replacement of Fujiwara Ginjiro by Yoshida Shigeru. Koiso's recruitment of Kobayashi Seizō and plans to consolidate official political associations are interpreted as an effort to create a Japanese-style fascist party and mobilize the country's nearly exhausted resources.

subfiles.title: Yoshida Shigeru and Andō Rikichi
subfiles.doc_type: translated biographical and political article; enclosure to despatch no. 264
subfiles.from: Supplement to Giefang Ribao, translated by the Co-ordinated Translation Center
subfiles.about: The article profiles Japan's new munitions minister and Taiwan's new governor-general as appointments made in response to the Allied advance.
subfiles.summary: Yoshida Shigeru is presented as a pro-military bureaucrat experienced in economic planning, labor mobilization, and wartime administration in Fukuoka and Kyushu. Andō Rikichi's army career is traced through operations in China and French Indochina to his appointment as governor-general of Taiwan. His selection is interpreted as evidence that Japan intended to strengthen Taiwan's land defenses against a possible American assault.

subfiles.title: The Japanese Today: The Decline of the Passion for War
subfiles.doc_type: translated newspaper article; enclosure to despatch no. 264
subfiles.from: Lin Ching, New Intelligence no. 64, supplement to Giefang Ribao
subfiles.about: The article compiles Japanese press evidence of declining confidence, resistance to labor controls, poor consumer goods, and malnutrition among schoolchildren.
subfiles.summary: Japanese commentators are quoted as warning that intellectuals doubted victory and that pessimism was spreading as military conditions and daily life deteriorated. Police statistics on supposedly wicked workers and students are interpreted as evidence of sabotage and resistance to labor conscription. Reports of rotten food, unusable brushes and toys, undernourished pupils, illness, and censorship of children's letters illustrate the collapse of civilian living standards.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 1599: Transmitting Memorandum of Conversation with a Former Attaché of the Romanian Legation at Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Embassy forwards a confidential memorandum based on a former Romanian diplomat's observations of Japan and North Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The despatch identifies the informant as a former Romanian Legation attaché who left Tokyo in January 1945 and spent about six weeks in North Manchuria while traveling toward the Soviet Union. It characterizes his information as broad rather than detailed but as a useful and generally reliable picture of conditions in Japan and Manchuria at the beginning of 1945.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation with Victor Gutzulesco
subfiles.doc_type: memorandum of conversation; enclosure to despatch no. 1599
subfiles.from: F. B. Stevens and J. Davies Jr.
subfiles.about: Former Romanian attaché Victor Gutzulesco reports on air raids, invasion defenses, morale, shortages, prisoners, and conditions in Japan, Korea, and Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Gutzulesco describes Tokyo's inadequate shelters and firefighting equipment, lightly equipped home-defense recruits, American prisoners employed in labor and broadcasting, and the shifting Japanese propaganda line as Germany's position worsened. He reports severe malnutrition, clothing and fuel shortages, dispersed home production, and a population that remained susceptible to official anti-American propaganda while becoming increasingly war-weary. Conditions in Korea appeared similar to those in Japan, whereas Japanese civilians and the Kwantung Army in Manchuria were better supplied; Chinese residents around Harbin and Manzhouli anticipated a Soviet entry after Japan's defeat.

subfiles.title: Letter concerning a list of political “moderates”
subfiles.about: Stettinius sends Forrestal a requested list of persons classified as political moderates and offers further information.
subfiles.summary: The brief letter follows a conversation held the previous day and encloses a list of individuals classified as “moderates.” Stettinius notes that the list may not fully meet Forrestal's needs and invites requests for additional information along the same lines.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 290: Communist and Other Publications Prepared by the American Coordinated Translation Center
subfiles.about: The Embassy forwards five newly mimeographed translations concerning Japanese politics and administration.
subfiles.summary: The despatch refers to earlier shipments of translations and reports that the Coordinated Translation Center had begun mimeographing its work sooner than expected. It encloses translations on Japanese political organization, the governor of Fukuoka, the Mongolian government's budget, a proposed Japanese fascist party, and Diet members' advocacy of a new party. Future mimeographed translations were to be transmitted without a covering despatch.

subfiles.title: The Two “Political Formulas”: Comments on the System of Cabinet Advisors and the Composite Planning Board
subfiles.doc_type: translated magazine article; enclosure to despatch no. 290
subfiles.from: Toshio Sumimoto, Jikyoku Joho, translated by the Co-ordinated Translation Center
subfiles.about: The article examines the Koiso Cabinet's advisory system and Composite Planning Board as machinery for accelerating wartime policy.
subfiles.summary: Sumimoto contrasts Koiso's governing formula with Tojo's concentration of authority and explains why criticism of weak coordination prompted creation of new consultative institutions. He traces proposals by Tanaka, Miura, and Sakomizu Hisatsune through the establishment of the Cabinet advisers on October 27 and the Composite Planning Board on November 1. Their delayed formation is criticized as evidence that the Cabinet could not keep pace with rapidly intensifying military operations around the Philippines; the article continues beyond page 109.
